bc_upper_gully.blurb: Upper Gully is a small sport wall at the south end of Area 44, north of Squamish. Six bolted routes run from 5.9 up to 5.11, split fairly evenly between the three grades, which makes it a fit for climbers who lead 5.10 and want a few harder options. The rock is highly featured though a little friable in places, so a helmet is a good idea. Belays are in the shade and the wall looks across to the Tantalus peaks. The base sits on a steep pile of talus and dirt, and getting up to it is a slog compared with the other walls here.

bc_insite_wall.blurb: Insite Wall is a sport wall within Area 44, close to Squamish. It holds six bolted routes, all of them 5.10, so it works well as a place to put in a string of climbs at one level. The lines are steep, running from just off vertical to mildly overhanging, on nicely featured rock that dries quickly. The wall catches direct sun later in the day and has comfortable belay spots with a view across to the Tantalus peaks. It is the third wall along the trail after the descent path, following the Corner and Preview Wall.

bc_huckleberry_lane.blurb: Huckleberry Lane is a compact, low-angle cliff in the Cal-Cheak climbing zone, on the road between Squamish and Whistler. It has six short routes: five bolted and one trad, mostly between 5.5 and 5.9, so it suits newer leaders and anyone wanting easy mileage. The climbing is slabby, with thin footholds on the hardest line. Big trees grow right up to the base, and the walk in is brief. Cal-Cheak as a whole gets morning shade and afternoon sun, so the cliff is a workable choice when the day is warm.
bc_huckleberry_lane.parking_note: Drive along the Daisy Lake Forest Service Road, passing the Cal-Cheak campground turnoff, then cross the single-lane bridge. About 2.4 km from the start, leave the car at the big basalt road cut on the right. The trail begins on the opposite side of the road.

bc_dione.blurb: Dione is a peak in the Tantalus Range of the Sea to Sky region near Squamish, with six alpine and trad routes. One is a much easier line; the other five fall in the 5.10 range, and the biggest line goes to around ten pitches. The start of the climbs involves crossing the glacier from the hut. The range is remote and known for glaciers, long days and frequent bad weather, so it is a destination for experienced alpine parties with their own rope-up and route-finding skills rather than a quick outing.

bc_wall_3.blurb: Wall 3 is part of Paradise Alley, a newer sport crag in the Squamish area. Six bolted routes sit here: two at 5.9, three around 5.11 and one at 5.12. The wall faces west, so it is best visited in the morning, before the sun reaches it in early afternoon. A trail runs through the middle of the crag, and the routes start on both sides of it. The left-hand lines begin from a platform that is simple to step onto from the left.
